posts.title: Why breakeven churn moves
posts.summary: A subscriber base can shrink while churn barely changes. The threshold that decides it isn't fixed.
posts.body:
Breakeven churn is the rate where new subscribers exactly replace lost ones. It's one division: **monthly gross adds ÷ the subscriber base**. Above that line the base shrinks, below it the base grows.

The mistake is treating it as a fixed target. It moves whenever either input moves, and the input that moves fastest is usually gross adds.

## What that looks like

Take a prepaid carrier adding about 215,000 subscribers a month against a 7.2 million base. Breakeven sits at 3.00%, so churn in the high 2s is fine and the base grows.

Now cut marketing spend. Gross adds fall to 187,000 a month, the base is roughly 7.4 million, and breakeven drops to 2.51%.

| Period | Gross adds | Base | Breakeven | Actual churn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First half | 215K | 7.2M | 3.00% | 2.75% |
| Second half | 187K | 7.4M | 2.51% | 2.82% |

Churn rose 7 basis points. The threshold fell 48. They crossed, and net adds went negative.

## Why it matters

Read only the churn rate and you'd conclude almost nothing changed. The damage came from the other side of the equation, and the churn number can't show it to you.

> A retention problem and an acquisition problem produce the same headline. They need different fixes.

posts.title: Two CAC rules that are the same rule
posts.summary: Payback under a third of tenure, and LTV:CAC above 3:1. These get quoted as separate tests. They can't disagree.
posts.body:
Two acquisition tests get quoted as if they're independent checks:

- Payback period under a third of average tenure
- LTV:CAC above 3:1

They're the same test. If payback is T/3, then CAC = m × T/3, where m is monthly contribution margin. LTV is m × T. So LTV ÷ CAC = (m × T) ÷ (m × T/3) = **exactly 3**.

Passing one always means passing the other. Quoting both doesn't add rigor.

## The part that does matter

The ceiling isn't fixed, because tenure isn't fixed. Tenure is 1 ÷ churn, so when churn rises, the maximum defensible CAC falls with it.

| Churn | Tenure | LTV | CAC ceiling |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.00% | 50 mo | $965 | $322 |
| 2.51% | 40 mo | $769 | $256 |
| 2.88% | 35 mo | $670 | $223 |
| 3.20% | 31 mo | $603 | $201 |

Spend to the ceiling at today's churn, then watch churn drift up, and you've bought subscribers at a price that only worked under the old rate.

So the sequencing writes itself: fix retention first, and the ceiling lifts on its own.

posts.title: The installed base is the asset
posts.summary: When hardware acquisition is effectively free, the growth question stops being how many devices you sell.
posts.body:
Most subscriber models start with acquisition cost. For a company where brand pull does the acquiring, that line is close to zero and the model has to start somewhere else.

If a device sells at a margin that covers itself immediately, the hardware isn't the investment. It's the entry point. What compounds afterward is whatever recurring revenue attaches to that device over its life.

## Rough shape of it

Assume a four-year replacement cycle and services revenue somewhere near $85–95 per device per year — derived by dividing total services revenue by the installed base, which is a crude estimate rather than a disclosed figure.

That puts services lifetime value around **$340–380 per device**, sitting on top of a hardware margin already captured at the point of sale.

## What follows

With billions of devices already in circulation, incremental growth from selling the next unit is small next to growth from raising attach rate on units already out there.

The installed base is the asset. Services is a measure of how much of it is actually being used.

posts.title: Failure
posts.summary: Learning to fail is the most valuable lesson in becoming successful.
posts.body:
Every model I have ever built has been wrong.

That is not modesty. It is arithmetic. A model is a set of
assumptions about a future that has not happened yet. Some
of those assumptions miss. The question was never whether
the model would be wrong. The question was by how much, in
which direction, and what that told me.

## Two kinds of wrong

There is the model that was wrong and taught you something.
The churn assumption was too optimistic. The CAC was based
on easy customers. The growth rate held right up until the
quarter it didn't.

Then there is the model that was never wrong, because it was
never tested against anything.

The second kind is worse. It costs nothing to be right about
a decision you never made.

## What a failure is

A failure is a receipt. It says something was spent — time,
money, a reputation, a weekend. It does not say the purchase
was a mistake. It says a purchase happened.

People with no failures are not more careful. They are less
exposed. They have arranged their lives so that nothing they
do can be checked.

## The part nobody says out loud

Most of the value comes from being wrong in a way you can
measure.

I have built startups. Done the product, done the design,
shipped the thing. Some of them never found users.

That failure is specific, and the specificity is what makes
it useful. It is not "the idea was bad." It is narrower: the
product worked and nobody adopted it. So the assumption
doing the most work was never the design. It was that
somebody out there was already waiting for this.

Building is the part I am good at. Adoption was the part I
was wrong about. I only know which was which because I built
it and watched.

You cannot get that from a win. A win is quiet. It confirms
what you already believed and hands you nothing new.

## So

Try the thing. Write the number down first, so you cannot
move it later. Then find out.

If you are right, you learned a little. If you are wrong,
you learned where the edge was.

The only outcome with nothing in it is the one where you
never put a number down at all.

posts.title: The future of AI and the possible implications on the economy.
posts.summary: With the growth of Anthropic and OpenAI how will their new product and iterations have an impact on employment and growth within the global economy.
posts.body: With Anthropic going public last week, we have seen some extreme measurements about what makes a strong company. The current stock price is based on future projections and its ability to meet revenue targets by 2030. I believe that the 1.5 trillion valuation assigned to Anthropic is high, I understand they have strong growth over the past 2 years but what they are building for companies will reduce the amount of human input leading to layoffs and then in turn higher unemployment. Then the unemployed will have lower free cash, so spending becomes tight. The companies that implement the AI agents will have a decline in revenue and profit due to amount of revenue or users because of low consumer spending. I see it being a double edged sword. We need to understand the speed at which we are attacking AI and evaluate the upside vs downside. We need to be able to build agents that help us progress in benefit of economic opportunity. We currently have a spending problem with the national debt and the interest payments. Perhaps implementing AI agents to refine the spending and ways to save would be more beneficial than having humans constantly run it which has been detrimental as we've seen.

The world economy at the end of 2026 is not heading into recession. It is settling into a regime of fragmented resilience. The IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026, down from 3.5% in 2025, with a rebound to 3.4% in 2027.
That headline hides two opposing forces: an AI investment boom propping up advanced-economy demand, and an energy shock from the war with Iran that began on 28 February. The result is a rare configuration — synchronized monetary tightening without a synchronized slowdown. My argument is that the binding constraint for 2027 is neither demand nor prices alone, but fiscal space.
Growth: divergence, not decline
Advanced economies are, unusually, accelerating while emerging markets slow. The IMF has advanced-economy growth edging up to 2.1% in 2026, while emerging and developing economies drop from 4.5% to 3.7%. The United States holds at 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, insulated as a net energy exporter and lifted by data-centre, chip and power investment. China slows to 4.5% and the euro area to 1.1%.
The geography of the shock explains the pattern. Middle East and Central Asia output contracts 0.3% in 2026, and energy-importing emerging economies absorb the terms-of-trade loss. In open-economy terms, this is a negative supply shock for importers and a positive income shock for exporters. That asymmetry keeps the global aggregate near 3% while dispersion widens.
 
Figure 1. Real GDP growth by region, 2025–2027 (IMF, October 2026).
Inflation and policy: the second tightening cycle
The energy shock has turned the 2024–25 easing cycle into a 2026 tightening cycle. Brent peaked near $126 in late March, was back above $115 in late October, and eased to about $92 by mid-November as Gulf exports recovered. Headline inflation followed, reaching 3.7% in the US, 3.8% in the euro area and 3.5% in the UK in September.
 
Figure 2. Brent crude, selected 2026 observations, against IMF reference levels.
Central banks have responded in near-unison. The Fed raised rates to 3.75–4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023. The ECB took its deposit rate to 2.50% over two hikes, and the Bank of England lifted Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November. The Bank of Canada hiked for the first time in over three years, and the Bank of Japan sits at 1.25%, a 31-year high.
 
Figure 3. Policy rates at the start of 2026 versus late November 2026.
The analytical question is second-round effects. Standard doctrine says to look through a supply shock unless expectations de-anchor. The ECB judges underlying inflation broadly stable and wages unresponsive, so its stance is closer to a precautionary hold. The Fed, by contrast, faces core CPI running 0.3% a month alongside third-quarter growth of 3.4% annualized: the shock is landing on demand that was already hot.
Real policy rates make the gap plain. Subtracting September headline inflation gives roughly +0.2 percentage points in the US and +0.5 in the UK, but about −1.3 in the euro area. Frankfurt is betting that the shock fades; Washington is not.
Fiscal space: the binding constraint
Public debt is the slow variable that now constrains every fast one. Global public debt reached about 94% of GDP in 2025, and the IMF projects it will exceed 100% before 2030, a level last seen after the Second World War. Interest costs have risen from 2% to nearly 3% of world GDP in four years. The global primary deficit, around 3.3% of GDP in 2026, sits well above the roughly 2.6% needed to stabilize debt.
The mechanics follow the standard debt-accumulation identity, where d is debt-to-GDP, r the effective interest rate, g nominal growth and pb the primary balance:
\Delta d_t = \frac{r_t - g_t}{1 + g_t}\, d_{t-1} - pb_t
A tightening cycle raises r just as the energy shock compresses real g for importers, so the r − g term turns against sovereigns from both sides. The United States is the clearest test: a general government deficit of 7–8% of GDP while operating near full capacity. If term premia keep rising, fiscal dominance stops being a theoretical worry and becomes a constraint on the Fed itself.
Trade, tariffs and currencies
Fragmentation is proving gradual and costly rather than abrupt. Some 2025 tariff rates were scaled back, and trade rerouted through third markets instead of collapsing; the IMF projects world trade volumes growing 4.6% in 2026. The cost shows up as accumulated efficiency losses, not a single bad year.
In currencies, rate differentials still dominate. The yen trades near 157 per dollar, only about 4% stronger than its 2026 low near 164, even with the Bank of Japan at a 31-year high. With Japanese real rates still negative, policy normalization has not yet closed the carry gap.
Outlook for 2027
The base case is a fragmented soft landing: global growth near 3.4%, inflation easing from 4.7% to 4.1%, and policy rates held at higher levels. Three risks dominate.
1.  Energy. The IMF's downside scenario puts oil at $130 from late 2026 into early 2027.
2.  The AI boom. Investment is straining power, chips and skilled labour, adding to inflation and valuation risk while productivity gains remain uneven.
3.  Fiscal. Higher-for-longer rates applied to record debt.
The upside, faster AI-driven productivity, is the one scenario that loosens all three constraints at once. For investors and policymakers alike, the variable to watch in 2027 is not the next rate decision but the term premium.
